summary: The inner loop of this CHI 2018 paper is a geometry-plus-polynomial pipeline (four ray casts from tracked body markers, offsets on a projection screen, a 15-parameter complete bivariate quartic fitted per angle, leave-one-out cross-validation) followed by two three-way RM-ANOVAs. All of it is re-implementable from the prose and is implemented and run here, but the authors released no pointing data and none of the ~240 fitted coefficients that are the paper's stated contribution, so no cell of Tables 1-3 can be recomputed from source. What can be checked without data was checked exhaustively: of 59 checks, all 35 derivations the paper's own tables can support hold (per-method mean offsets, the LOOCV correction percentages including the 29.3% headline, the Study 2 improvements of 13.1% and 4.5%, the cross-paper ratios against Mayer et al. 2015, and every design count), 4 more are not derivable from anything published, and 6 of the 20 reported F/p pairs fail recomputation - including a main effect the paper calls significant, ENVIRONMENT on accuracy, reported as F(1,15)=1.3, p=.027 where that F gives p=.272. The outer loop is two lab studies with 36 participants wearing an HTC Vive under an OptiTrack rig; it was not attempted, not simulated and not scored, and the paper's human findings are neither confirmed nor disputed here.

boundary.claim: Four ray casts (EFRC, IFRC, FRC, HRC) constructed from tracked markers and intersected with the projection screen
boundary.evidence: Implemented in src/geometry.py; exact on the 7x5 grid and on the angle round-trip (python src/selftest.py). Cannot be checked against the paper: the marker-to-anatomy transforms (cyclops eye from HMD markers, 'true finger tip' from marker plus per-user measurement, forearm centre 'approximating the forearm with a frustum of a cone') are prose only, and no marker data was released.

boundary.claim: Preprocessing: 100-900 ms sample window, offset defined as ray-screen intersection to target, two-standard-deviation outlier bound, head alignment across participants
boundary.evidence: Implemented in src/preprocess.py and run end to end (./run_all.sh; 32,111 synthetic trials survive filtering). Three of the four steps are under-specified (decisions D1-D4) and the paper never reports how many trials the filter removed, so no count can be matched.

boundary.claim: Average offset per ray cast over both environments: 9.33 cm EFRC, 28.09 cm IFRC, 65.0 cm FRC, 42.46 cm HRC
boundary.evidence: Recomputed from Table 1 to within 0.005 cm for all four methods (python src/check_paper.py, ids s1-mean-*).
boundary.citation: Accuracy of Ray Casts, p. 5, from Table 1

boundary.claim: The correction model family f1-f4, with f4 the 15-parameter function of Equation 1, fitted by a nonlinear least-squares solver
boundary.evidence: The 15 terms of Equation 1 are exactly the complete bivariate quartic; the basis is reconstructed term by term and asserted in src/selftest.py. The model is linear in x0..x14, and the paper's nonlinear solver agrees with a linear least-squares solve to 6.5e-10, so the stated solver choice is immaterial.

boundary.claim: The fitted correction models themselves: 4 ray casts x 2 environments x 2 angles x 15 coefficients
boundary.evidence: Blocker: never published, in the paper or at any of the 22 locations searched (SOURCES.md). The paper's headline contribution therefore cannot be applied by a reader even in principle. The predecessor paper did print its coefficients (Mayer et al. 2015, Table 3); they are re-implemented here in src/mayer2015_model.py to show what the missing artifact would look like.

boundary.claim: LOOCV correction achieved: FRC 55.9%, IFRC 50.1%, EFRC 10.9%, HRC 0.2%, overall 29.3%; remaining offsets 8.2, 14.0, 28.6, 42.3 cm
boundary.evidence: All nine figures reproduce from Table 1 (check ids s1-correction-*, s1-remaining-*, s1-correction-overall): the per-method value is the mean of the two per-environment percentages and the overall value is the mean of those four. The aggregation order and the CV granularity are unstated (D5, D6).

mismatch.reported: EFRC correction 10.9%, HRC remaining offset 42.3 cm
mismatch.observed: 10.96% and 42.385 cm; the paper truncates rather than rounds, here and in about six other derived figures

boundary.claim: Four one-way RM-ANOVAs comparing RealWorld with VirtualReality per ray cast (EFRC F(1,19)=5.845 p=.026; IFRC F=.447 p=.512; FRC F=33.13 p<.001; HRC F=31.48 p<.001)
boundary.evidence: Blocker: the 8,400 postures were never released, so no F can be recomputed. All four reported F/p pairs are internally consistent, which is the most that can be established from the text.

boundary.claim: Fatigue checks: raw-TLX means per session and a one-way RM-ANOVA in each study, both non-significant
boundary.evidence: Study 1's F(3,57)=.047, p=.986 is internally consistent and its df match 20 participants over 4 sessions. Study 2's is not, on two counts (see mismatch). The conclusion drawn (no fatigue effect) is a null result that neither error overturns.

mismatch.reported: F(5,15) = .654, p = .659 for six raw-TLX sessions with 16 participants
mismatch.observed: the design implies error df = 75, not 15 (Study 1 uses the analogous F(3,57) correctly); and F(5,15) = .654 gives p = .663

boundary.claim: Study 2 condition tables - TCT (Table 2) and remaining offset (Table 3) - produced under a design that collapses 8 factorial cells into 6 administered conditions
boundary.evidence: The design's fingerprint is visible in the paper's own numbers: with no cursor a participant cannot perceive whether correction is applied, and Table 2's no-cursor TCT is identical across CORRECTION in both environments (1.48/1.48 and 1.64/1.64), exactly as the collapse requires (check ids s2-tct-nocursor-identical-*). Table 3's no-cursor offsets do differ, as they must, since correction still moves the computed intersection.

boundary.claim: Correction improvements: 13.1% overall without a cursor, 16.3% RealWorld, 9.5% VirtualWorld, 4.5% with a cursor
boundary.evidence: All four reproduce from Table 3 (check ids s2-improve-*). The two aggregate figures come out at 13.1% and 4.5% only if the cell means are pooled before the ratio is taken; averaging the two per-environment percentages instead gives 12.98% and 4.31% (decision D14).
boundary.citation: Discussion p. 9 and Conclusion, from Table 3

boundary.claim: Two three-way RM-ANOVAs over CORRECTION x CURSOR x ENVIRONMENT, on accuracy and on task completion time
boundary.evidence: The analysis is re-implemented (src/pipeline.py:study2 using statsmodels AnovaRM) and runs on study-2-shaped data, reproducing the F(1,15) structure the paper's df imply. The paper's values cannot be recomputed (no trials released), and 5 of the 14 reported F/p pairs fail recomputation.

mismatch.reported: 'a significant effect of ... ENVIRONMENT, F(1,15) = 1.3, p = .027 on the participants' pointing accuracy', restated as a finding in the Discussion
mismatch.observed: F(1,15) = 1.3 gives p = .272; on the printed F the effect is not significant. Four further pairs also fail: accuracy CORRECTION p = .027 vs .036; accuracy CORRECTION x ENVIRONMENT p = .36 vs .337; TCT ENVIRONMENT p = .956 vs .950; TCT CURSOR x ENVIRONMENT reported p < .001 vs .00128
mismatch.delta: p +.245 on ENVIRONMENT; flips the significance decision at alpha = .05

boundary.claim: Square target sizes holding 90% of pointing actions: 17.6 cm (no cursor, RW), 18.8 cm (no cursor, VR), 4.1 cm and 4.5 cm with cursor, and the per-condition shrinks of 6.9, 11.6, 6.5 and 8.9%
boundary.evidence: Blocker: needs the per-trial two-dimensional endpoints; Table 3 publishes only the mean and SD of the scalar distance, from which a square capture region is not recoverable. The estimator is implemented and validated against its analytic value (src/pipeline.py:target_size_90; selftest gives 11.69 cm vs 11.69 cm). Forcing an isotropic Rayleigh assumption onto Table 3 - my assumption, not the paper's - would give 22.0 cm where the paper reports 17.6 cm.

boundary.claim: Targets can on average be 8.5% smaller when the correction models are applied
boundary.evidence: Mean of the paper's own four per-condition shrinks (6.9, 11.6, 6.5, 8.9) = 8.475% (check id s2-target-shrink-mean).

boundary.claim: Comparison with the predecessor study: errors before correction 4.8x (EFRC), 1.9x (IFRC) and 3.7x (FRC) larger in Mayer et al. 2015; IFRC 89.2% larger than EFRC after correction here; EFRC 4.9% larger than IFRC there
boundary.evidence: All five numbers reproduce against Mayer et al. 2015 Tables 1-2, row 'standing 2m', and against Table 1 here (check ids s1-ratio-2015-*, s1-ifrc-vs-efrc, s1-2015-efrc-vs-ifrc).

mismatch.reported: 'Overall Mayer et al. reported errors before correction 4.8 times larger for EFRC, 1.9 for IFRC and 3.7 for FRC'
mismatch.observed: 4.76, 1.90, 3.69 if 'overall' means the RealWorld column alone; 5.21, 1.97, 3.43 if it means the average over both environments, which is how 'overall' is used elsewhere in the paper
mismatch.delta: +0.41 on EFRC under the other reading

boundary.claim: Design and sample arithmetic: 7x5 = 35 targets, 35 x 6 x 2 = 420 trials, x 20 participants = 8,400 postures, 420/4 = 105 gestures per session, 6 conditions x 35 x 2 = 420 trials in Study 2, grid spacing = screen dimension / (n-1)
boundary.evidence: Every count closes exactly (check ids design-*), including the spacing: 269.4/6 = 44.9 cm and 136.2/4 = 34.05 cm, which also recovers the digit the PDF's text layer drops in '34.cm'.
boundary.citation: Study Design pp. 3-4 and p. 7; Apparatus p. 4; Results p. 5

boundary.claim: Data-collection study: 20 participants (4 female, M = 22.1 years), 420 mid-air pointing gestures each, in a real room and in a VR replica, tracked by OptiTrack with 7 rigid bodies
boundary.evidence: Requires human participants: the measurement is where a person freely chooses to point when asked to point as they naturally would. Not attempted and not simulated.

boundary.claim: Evaluation study: 16 new participants in a 2x2x2 within-subjects selection task validating the correction models in real time
boundary.evidence: Requires human participants; the effects of interest (cursor, correction, environment) are defined only relative to human behaviour. Not attempted and not simulated.

boundary.claim: Raw NASA-TLX administered after every session in both studies as a fatigue and workload check
boundary.evidence: Subjective workload can only be reported by a participant.

boundary.claim: Eye-dominance screening of every participant with the Miles and Porta tests
boundary.evidence: A physical perceptual test administered to a person.

boundary.claim: Fourteen participant-specific anthropometric measurements and the avatar dimensions and bone structure fitted from them
boundary.evidence: An experimenter measuring a body with a tape and a laser measurement tool before the session.

boundary.claim: Informed consent and demographic questionnaire at the start of each session
boundary.evidence: Human research procedure.

boundary.claim: Recruitment and eligibility: university volunteer pool, right-handed only, no locomotor coordination problems
boundary.evidence: Sampling humans.

decisions.question: How are the samples inside the 100-900 ms window combined into a single pointing posture?
decisions.where: Preprocessing, p. 5: 'we used the samples between 100ms and 900ms' - a window is given, an aggregator is not
decisions.assumed: Arithmetic mean of every tracked coordinate, then cast the ray (mean-then-cast, not cast-then-mean)
decisions.sensitivity: Moderate. The two orders differ by second-order terms in the tremor amplitude the paper itself discusses (8-12 Hz); negligible for EFRC, larger for IFRC and FRC where 1 degree of direction error is about 3.5 cm on the screen at 2 m

decisions.question: Is the 100-900 ms window measured from the button press or from target onset?
decisions.where: Procedure, p. 5: participants 'click ... when they started to hold a gesture' and 'the target disappeared after one second' - both define a plausible zero
decisions.assumed: From the button press that starts the one-second hold
decisions.sensitivity: Moderate. Anchoring at target onset would place part of the window in the movement phase and inflate every offset

decisions.question: Over which grouping is the two-standard-deviation outlier bound computed, and is it one- or two-sided?
decisions.where: Preprocessing, p. 5: 'using two times the standard deviation as an upper bound', with no grouping
decisions.assumed: Per ray cast x environment x target, one-sided on the distance, following the predecessor paper's explicit rule
decisions.sensitivity: Moderate and unfalsifiable: global versus per-target filtering changes both the retained N and the mean offsets, and the paper reports neither the retained N nor the removal count

decisions.question: What transform does 'we aligned the heads of the participants' apply?
decisions.where: Preprocessing, p. 5
decisions.assumed: Translate every tracked position of a participant by (grand-mean head position - that participant's mean head position)
decisions.sensitivity: High for the fit: it defines the shared frame the universal polynomial lives in. A vertical-only shift, a full rigid alignment or a per-trial re-centring all yield different alpha distributions and therefore different coefficients

decisions.question: Is the leave-one-out cross-validation leave-one-participant-out or leave-one-trial-out?
decisions.where: Modeling, p. 6: 'we used leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)'
decisions.assumed: Leave-one-participant-out, following the predecessor paper, which states it explicitly; exposed as --cv participant|trial
decisions.sensitivity: High. Leave-one-trial-out leaks each participant's own bias into training and inflates the apparent correction; the paper's claim is a user-independent model, which only leave-one-participant-out supports

decisions.question: In what order are the correction percentages aggregated - per environment then per method, or pooled over all trials?
decisions.where: Modeling, p. 6, which prints one percentage per method and one overall
decisions.assumed: Mean of the two per-environment percentages, then the mean over the four methods
decisions.sensitivity: Low but decisive for reproduction: this reading recovers 29.3% exactly, whereas pooling the cell means first gives 29.5%

decisions.question: What reference frame defines alpha_pitch and alpha_yaw?
decisions.where: Modeling, p. 6: angles 'between the ray cast and the body'; 'the body' is never defined
decisions.assumed: World axes with +z the screen normal and the origin at the ray root
decisions.sensitivity: High. A shoulder- or head-anchored frame rotates the domain of the polynomial, so coefficients are not transferable between conventions - and since none were published, a reader cannot detect the mismatch

decisions.question: Which model family, fitted to which data, does Study 2 apply in real time?
decisions.where: Apparatus, p. 7: 'the Unity scene was adjusted to support our model if needed'
decisions.assumed: f4, per environment, for EFRC, fitted on all 20 Study-1 participants
decisions.sensitivity: Moderate; this is the assumption most favourable to the paper, since f4 on all data is the strongest form of the model

decisions.question: Was the correction used in Study 2 the cross-validated model or the all-data fit?
decisions.where: Not stated anywhere in Evaluation, pp. 7-8
decisions.assumed: The all-data fit
decisions.sensitivity: Moderate. Either is user-independent with respect to the 16 new participants, but the all-data fit is better trained, so a LOOCV-based deployment would likely have shown a smaller improvement than 13.1%

decisions.question: What instant of a Study-2 trial defines the recorded pointing endpoint?
decisions.where: Evaluation, p. 7 defines TCT by the button press but never ties the accuracy measure to an instant
decisions.assumed: The ray-screen intersection at the moment of the click
decisions.sensitivity: High in the with-cursor conditions, where participants actively null their error: averaging a hold window instead would report a smaller offset than an instantaneous sample

decisions.question: What are the cursor's size, update rate and smoothing?
decisions.where: Apparatus, p. 7: 'a green crosshair as suggested by Olsen and Nielsen', with a 30 FPS tracking system stated on p. 4
decisions.assumed: Not implemented; this repository renders nothing
decisions.sensitivity: High for the paper's own result: cursor gain, latency and smoothing directly determine the 1.1-1.3 cm with-cursor offsets and the TCT increase the abstract claims

decisions.question: Do the ANOVAs run on per-participant cell means, and was the skew of a distance measure addressed?
decisions.where: Results, p. 8
decisions.assumed: Per-participant cell means (the reported error df of 15 with 16 participants implies it); no transform, matching the paper's silence
decisions.sensitivity: Low for the df, moderate for the p-values: Euclidean distances are right-skewed and bounded below at zero, so an untransformed RM-ANOVA is anti-conservative

decisions.question: How is raw TLX scored - which subscales and what range?
decisions.where: Procedure, p. 5 and Results, p. 8: 'a raw NASA-Task Load Index (raw TLX)'
decisions.assumed: Unweighted mean of the six standard subscales on 0-100, consistent with the reported means of 35-40
decisions.sensitivity: Low: the fatigue conclusion is a null result on either scoring

decisions.question: Is the reported improvement a pooled ratio or a mean of per-environment ratios?
decisions.where: Discussion, p. 9: 'the models overall improvement without a cursor was 13.1%'
decisions.assumed: Pool the cell means first, then take the ratio - the only reading that yields 13.1% and 4.5%
decisions.sensitivity: Low in magnitude (13.16% versus 12.98%), but it is the difference between reproducing the paper's figure and missing it

decisions.question: How is the 90%-capture square defined - centred on the target or on the mean endpoint, per-axis or radial, empirical or parametric?
decisions.where: Accuracy, p. 8: 'we will estimate target sizes to fit at least 90% of the mid-air pointing actions ... For simplicity we only fit a squared target shape'
decisions.assumed: Centred on the target, per-axis, empirical 90th percentile of max(|dx|,|dy|)
decisions.sensitivity: High. Centring on the mean endpoint removes the residual bias and shrinks every reported size by several cm; this is exactly the number a designer would act on

decisions.question: How were target order and condition order randomised, and with what seed?
decisions.where: Study Design, p. 4 ('the order of the targets was randomized while the order of ENVIRONMENT was counter-balanced') and Procedure, p. 7 ('CORRECTION and CURSOR were randomized within ENVIRONMENT')
decisions.assumed: Uniform random target order per condition; no seed is recoverable
decisions.sensitivity: Low for the means, moderate for order effects: randomising rather than counterbalancing CORRECTION x CURSOR leaves learning confounded with condition across a six-condition, one-hour session

decisions.question: How are participants whose eye dominance was 'unclear' (4 of 20, 5 of 16) treated in the cyclops-eye construction?
decisions.where: Participants, pp. 5 and 8 - the screening is reported, its use never is
decisions.assumed: Treated identically; the cyclops eye is the midpoint between the eyes for everyone
decisions.sensitivity: Low for the construction itself, but it renders the screening decorative: eye dominance is measured, reported, and then enters no model or analysis

decisions.question: How many trials survived the outlier filter?
decisions.where: Never reported; only the 8,400 postures collected (Results, p. 5)
decisions.assumed: Unknown; the synthetic run retains about 95%
decisions.sensitivity: Unfalsifiable: without the retained N neither Table 1's SDs nor any effect size can be validated, and the predecessor paper did report its removal counts

decisions.question: What exactly is the vertical target spacing?
decisions.where: Apparatus, p. 4, printed as '34.cm' - a digit is lost in the PDF text layer
decisions.assumed: 34.05 cm, recovered as 136.2 / (5 - 1)
decisions.sensitivity: None: the reconstruction is exact and consistent with the horizontal spacing, 269.4 / (7 - 1) = 44.9 cm

decisions.question: Does the choice of solver matter, given the paper fits a parameter-linear model with a 'nonlinear least-squares solver'?
decisions.where: Modeling, p. 6
decisions.assumed: Both implemented and compared: --solver lstsq and --solver nls
decisions.sensitivity: None, and this is a positive finding: predictions agree to 6.5e-10 (src/selftest.py), so the paper's unusual solver choice cannot explain any discrepancy
